#2653. Group of retired MLB umpires, including Joe West, file lawsuit alleging they are owed more than $2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former MLB umpire Joe West is part of a group of five retired umpires who are suing their pension plan and alleging they have been underpaid by the plan, the Associated Press reports. West, along with Tom Hallion, Gerry Davis, Larry Vanover, and Jerry Layne, filed the suit in late September in federal court in New York.

The suit alleges that the five umpires have been underpaid by the pension plan by more than $2 million. According to the AP, the suit "was filed against the American Leagues and National Leagues of Professional Baseball Clubs Retirement Income Plan for Umpires and that entity's retirement committee." The five umpires claim their benefits were not calculated correctly and therefore should receive additional money.

West, 74, retired from umpiring in MLB in 2021 after umpiring more than 5,000 games at the highest level starting in 1976. The man they called "Cowboy Joe" umpired a record 5,460 games in all, was known as a colorful figure in the sport and sometimes even a source of controversy.

In 2021, West won more than $500,000 in damages as the result of a defamation suit against former MLB player Paul Lo Duca after Lo Duca alleged during a podcast that West would "open up the strike zone" for reliever Billy Wagner in exchange for driving one of Wagner's vintage cars.

West referenced his "history with lawsuits" on Thursday. From the AP:

West said that when he brought up the issue to the retirement committee, he was offered a relatively small sum. West said MLB senior vice president and chief employment counsel Steven Gonzalez told him: "If you don't like the number, sue us."

"Does Steve Gonzalez not know my history with dealing with lawsuits?" West said.

Like West, Davis also retired after the 2021 season while Hallion umpired through the 2022 season and Layne and Vanover stepped away after the 2024 campaign. The five sued as individuals and did not involve the umpires' union, their lawyer, Paul B. Holmes, said, per the AP.

A pretrial conference in the case is scheduled for Dec. 11.

#2652. Bengals nearly made a costly trade-deadline blunder, and Zac Taylor had to explain it

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There were six trades on trade deadline day Tuesday, but a trade that didn't happen provided one of the more entertaining moments of what was already a wild day.

The Bengals agreed to send a sixth-round pick to the Eagles for edge defender Arnold Ebiketie, a fairly run-of-the-mill deal on the surface: Ebiketie figured to join the Bengals' pass-rush rotation with Cashius Howell (wrist) on IR. But it seemed the Bengals failed to realize or understand that the trade would have meant also forfeiting the compensatory 2027 third-round pick they are due after losing Trey Hendrickson in free agency.

The trade fell through after the Bengals, it seems, learned about that part of the equation. Wednesday, Bengals coach Zac Taylor addressed the near-trade.

"I feel good (about the EDGE depth)," Taylor said. "Obviously we tried something yesterday, and [director of personnel] Duke [Tobin] was very explicit with me when he came and spoke to me of how he wanted this portrayed, and I'm not comfortable doing it, but I'm going to do what he asked.

"We did make an effort to kind of put some depth in there in place of Cashius. As we got into it, obviously it was going to be a little more costly than we initially anticipated. He's really apologetic about it and wants to make clear Philly was a great trade partner. It was on our, and that's just the way things go, but certainly have a ton of confidence in our front office and how they do things, and they've given us the players that have allowed us to be 6-2 right now and playing at such a high level. So, we'll put that behind us and move forward ..."

Nick Korte, who contributes to the contract source site OverTheCap, was first to point the potential snafu out. The Eagles signed Ebiketie as a compensatory free agent this offseason, meaning he counted against the compensatory pick formula. That status carries over if he is traded in-season, per the Collective Bargaining Agreement. Here's the full chart:

Oh that's brutal on the 3rd round comp pick! as noted by @nickkorte pic.twitter.com/OwwyNB71PA

The Bengals may have believed Cordell Volson counted as a CFA lost, but he has not played this year, rendering his departure moot in the compensatory picks balance.

To his credit, Taylor said the failed trade didn't interrupt his Tuesday preparation, aside from the very brief conversation he had with Tobin, and that it would not impact the team's preparation for a crucial Week 10 "Sunday Night Football" matchup with the Steelers. Cincinnati and Pittsburgh are tied for the AFC North lead at 6-2.

The Bengals ended up not making any in-season trades this year, even while most other top AFC teams, including the Jaguars, Chiefs and Broncos, did. Taylor had a lot of confidence in the group he has, which has won four straight.

"I really like where we're at," Taylor said. "I think Duke really likes where we're at. So this is a team with a lot of confidence right now. I know it's a fun period of time, the weeks leading up to the trade deadline, for fans and people to generate a lot of media attention of of it, but the truth is we really do like where we're at."

#2648. Ex-Guardians catcher Bo Naylor testifies in defense of Emmanuel Clase, Luis Ortiz in MLB pitch-rigging trial

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Cleveland Guardians catcher Bo Naylor on Thursday testified in federal court that he perceived nothing untoward about disputed pitches thrown by former All-Star closer Emmanuel Clase and his former Guardians teammate Luis Ortiz, ESPN reports.

Naylor, who played five seasons for the Guardians, appeared as a witness for the defense in the ongoing federal trial in which prosecutors allege that Clase and Ortiz rigged multiple pitches for the benefit of co-conspiring bettors. In Clase's case, he's alleged to have done so in 17 games across a two-year period beginning in May 2023. Naylor, now a member of the Milwaukee Brewers, was catcher for some of Clase's disputed appearances during that span, including seven of the 18 pitches he's alleged to have rigged.

Naylor, a defense witness, was shown video replays of some of the pitches the government alleges were predetermined by Clase or Ortiz as part of the scheme. Naylor was behind the plate for many of them and said they looked like common sliders outside the strike zone. He said the scouting reports on the hitters Ortiz faced during the two pitches in question indicated that sliders low and away would be a "weapon."

In November 2025, Clase and Ortiz were indicted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York. According to the Department of Justice, both pitchers "agreed in advance with their co-conspirators to throw specific types of pitches and speeds of pitches." The Department of Justice alleged that the pair made at least $450,000 by rigging outings and throwing specific pitches to benefit bettors who wagered on the outcomes of those pitches.

Both Clase and Ortiz pleaded not guilty to those charges in November of last year. Clase and Ortiz have been on administrative leave since late June 2025 while Major League Baseball investigates. MLB has the authority to discipline the pitchers regardless of how the criminal trial plays out.

The pair could face up to 65 years in prison if convicted on the charges of wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery, and money laundering conspiracy.

#2645. Cavaliers coach Kenny Atkinson explains infamous 'analytically' quote during playoffs loss to Knicks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NBA players regularly draw scrutiny for things they say to the press, but coaches tend to be reserved enough to avoid getting too much egg on their faces. Kenny Atkinson is a recent exception; the Cleveland Cavaliers coach has been mocked for the past six months or so for his now-infamous comments after Game 3 of the Eastern Conference Finals.

With the Cavaliers down 3-0 to the New York Knicks, Atkinson was asked how he could give hope to his players, as no team in NBA history has ever overcome a 3-0 series deficit. "Analytically … we've won 2 out of 3," Atkinson said at the time. "We're two out of the three in the expected score. If you believe in process and all that, like, man, take that later. I don't throw that on them. I see it for myself, and if I have this feeling, I can go to our analytical table and be like, man, the expected score was like one point or two — us shooting way below expected, them shooting way over."

As Atkinson explained, analytics can estimate what a game's score should have been based on the shots both teams managed to produce and the expected field goal percentage of those shots. Essentially, if both teams shot exactly as the numbers suggest they would over a long sample, this is what the score would be. Atkinson did not specify which games he meant out of the three, but it was likely Game 1, which Cleveland lost in overtime, and Game 3, which New York won, 121-113. Prime Stats has an expected score metric that had Game 3 at a 113-113 tie, and while New York had an expected 10-point win in Game 1, that accounts for overtime. If the actual score had matched what Cleveland's analytics department projected in regulation, the game never would have gotten an extra period and the Cavaliers would have gone up 1-0.

Obviously, despite the expected scores, the Knicks led the series 3-0 at that point and had won those games by 40 total points. They went on to win Game 4 by 37 points, 130-93, though if it's any consolation, the Prime Stats expected score was a slightly less embarrassing 125-100. Both before the Game 4 sweep and afterward, Atkinson's quote was widely mocked. That includes jabs by multiple Knicks, as Josh Hart joked that "I guess we lost analytically" on his podcast with Jalen Brunson, and Karl-Anthony Towns, who said before the ESPYs that "analytically, we should win" the Best Team award. The word "analytically" has become shorthand for anyone attempting to justify an ugly defeat using numbers.

On Saturday, the Cavaliers faced the Knicks for the first time since that series. New York won again, 109-97, and yet again, the expected score was slightly more favorable to Cleveland, with Prime Stats posting an expected score of 112-103. Atkinson did not point to those numbers after Saturday's defeat. Instead, he attempted to explain the widely derided quote, arguing that the quote was taken out of context, which made the soundbite sound less flattering than his actual answer was.

"I would just say there was no coach more complimentary of the Knicks and honest about our performance and how they dominated us," Atkinson told reporters. "So you live and learn a little bit with those things. But like I said, 99% of my comments were how they dominated us. They were by far the better team. I answered the question, as it was taken, [which was] 'And you're down 3-0, what hope do you have of even giving to your guys?'

"We get a lot of information … and I wasn't lying in that sense, but in no sense was it like, 'Oh, man, we deserve to be winning.' Like zero — zero — thought of that."

Atkinson acknowledged that "no one wants to hear" about process when the outcome is a blown 22-point fourth-quarter lead and a 3-0 deficit, but he was trying to figure out how to rally his troops in an impossible situation. His phrasing has become a meme, but when you're down 3-0 in the playoffs, you'll grasp at any signs of positivity you can find. Atkinson had numbers suggesting the two teams were closer than the scoreboard suggested. Using those numbers to try to inspire his team made sense. Putting them out there in public risked exactly the sort of ridicule he ultimately got. The soundbite eclipsed the quote and the context, and the rest is history.

The market for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the offseason's best free agent, is already hot, according to the New York Post. We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available this offseason, and the best available position player. Young had been speculated as a trade candidate since last offseason, but the new extension locks him in as part of Washington's long-term core.

The NFL trade deadline was Tuesday, and no one made a bigger move than the Minnesota Vikings. With their season hanging in the balance, the Vikings decided to make a trade for Kirk Cousins.

If that happens, it would mark the first time in NFL history that a division has sent all four of its teams to the playoffs in one season.

So who else is projected to get in? Glad you asked.

To help us figure that out, we had our analytics expert, Stephen Oh, simulate the rest of the 2026 season. There are 136 games left on the regular-season schedule, along with 13 playoff games, and Oh simulated all of them. Not only did he project all eight division winners and the 14 playoff teams, but he also crowned a Super Bowl champion.

With that in mind, let's get to the projections. And just as a reminder, we're projecting what the NFL playoff field will look like at the end of the season. This is NOT the current playoff standings.

The AFC playoff picture is starting to take shape, and based on our projection, it's starting to feel like the playoff teams in this conference are almost locked in at this point. For the second straight week, not only does our projection have the same seven teams making the playoffs, but they're all seeded in the exact same spot.

Here's the projected AFC playoff field (with each team's current record):  1. Bills (7-1) -- AFC East champion 2. Jaguars (6-2) -- AFC South champion 3. Broncos (7-2) -- AFC West champion 4. Bengals (6-2) -- AFC North champion 5. Chiefs (6-2) 6. Steelers (6-2) 7. Patriots (5-4) JUST MISSED: Texans (3-5), Browns (5-4)

According to our projection, the only real battle will be for the seventh seed. We have the Patriots projected to get the spot right now, but the Texans are nipping at their heels. The good news for the Vikings is that adding Kirk Cousins does help: They're now projected to finish with 11 wins — compared to 10 without Cousins — but the problem is that 11 wins won't help them win the division. Here's the projected NFC playoff field (with each team's current record):  1. 49ers (7-1) -- NFC West champion 2. Lions (6-2) -- NFC North champion 3. Giants (5-2-1) -- NFC East champion 4. Buccaneers (3-6) -- NFC South champion 5. Bears (7-2) 6. Vikings (6-2) 7. Packers (6-3)  JUST MISSED: Seahawks (5-4), Rams (5-4)

For the first time all season, our model is projecting ALL FOUR NFC North teams to make the playoffs. At this point, it feels like the only way that's not going to happen is if the Rams or Seahawks get to 11 wins, but our computer doesn't see that happening.

Having all four teams from a single division make the postseason in the same year wasn't possible until 2020, when the NFL expanded the playoffs to 14 teams. Since then, there have been several instances where a division has put three teams in, but we still haven't seen a division put all four of its teams in, so this could be a history-making season.

AFC breakdown: Homefield advantage ends up being an actual advantage here, with all three home teams winning in the opening round. With the Patriots and Chiefs going out, they would eliminate the two teams that have represented the AFC in eight of the past nine Super Bowls.

NFC breakdown: The NFC North has been the best division in football all year, and the division makes a statement in the wild-card round by producing three winners. After watching the home teams sweep through the wild-card round, the run continues with Buffalo and Jacksonville both winning at home. With the win, the Bills advance to their third AFC title game since 2020 while the Jaguars make a return trip to the AFC Championship for the first time since 2017.

NFC breakdown: The Lions beat an NFC North team in the wild-card round, and they continue their postseason run by beating another NFC North team in the divisional round. As for the 49ers, Kyle Shanahan figures out a way to get his offense going against Minnesota's tough defense, propelling his team to a win. This sets up a rematch of the 2023 NFC title game between the Lions and 49ers.

If you're scoring at home, we are now down to four teams: Three teams that have never won a Super Bowl (Bills, Jaguars and Lions) and one team that hasn't won a Super Bowl in over 30 years (the 49ers' last title came in 1994)

We've been doing a projection every week since the start of the season, and here's a look at the projected Super Bowl each week.

As you can see, the computer has really taken a liking to the Bills, as this marks the third straight week Buffalo is projected to win the Super Bowl. Scratch that, the computer actually loves the Bills: Buffalo has a 16.94% chance of winning it all, which is a huge number when you consider there's only one other team that's even above 10% (the Jaguars are at 10.74%).

#2641. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2640. Five under-the-radar MLB free agents who could make a big impact next season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a little more than a week old now and we're still waiting for the first big trade or free agent signing. That isn't unusual, though. The hot stove, like the regular season, is a marathon, not a sprint. A lockout is expected when the collective bargaining agreement ends at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and there should be a flurry of activity before then.

We ranked the offseason's top 50 free agents, and although it is not a great class, there are dozens of quality players available. You just have to know where to look. Here now are five players who did not rank among our top 50 free agents, but would nonetheless be good options and solid pickups for teams that want to raise their floor and improve their supporting cast.

It was a tale of two seasons for the 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, who had a 5.81 ERA before the All-Star break and a 1.71 ERA after. The under-the-hood estimators, like FIP and xERA, were better in the second half as well, though Abreu lost close to 2 mph off his fastball this year and, not coincidentally, a whole bunch of swings and misses. Abreu is third in appearances and second in innings among relievers since 2022 and it's possible the workload is catching up to him. There's still enough bat-missing ability and late-inning experience here for Abreu to contribute to a contender's bullpen. It just might happen as a seventh-inning guy moving forward, not as the Moment of Truth™ reliever who pitches in the game's biggest moments.

If you're looking for a bottom of the order guy who will take walks and give you 10-15 home runs, that's J.P. Crawford. His defense, specifically his range and arm, has slipped so much in his early 30s that he's no longer a viable shortstop, though he played 33 games at third base this past season. I like him better at second base, but third base works too. Crawford gets on-base at a decent clip and won't strike out excessively, plus he's long been regarded as an excellent teammate and grade-A clubhouse guy. It seems like his time with the Mariners is over and it's for the best. Crawford can go elsewhere, play a new position, and just be part of the lineup rather than one of the faces of the franchise.

Due to injury and ineffectiveness, it looked like Sean Newcomb was on his way out of baseball two years ago. He then reinvented himself as a sinker/curveball guy and carved out a nice second phase to his career as a workhorse utility reliever who won't beat himself with walks (an early career bugaboo) and will limit hard contact in the air. Newcomb, 33, worked at least 90 innings the last two seasons while pitching in every possible role. He closed out games, worked high leverage as a setup guy, soaked up innings in long relief, and opened a few times as well. Newcomb is likely miscast as a go-to bullpen option, though he can be a valuable third or fourth option for a contender. The utility reliever is all the rage these days and Newcomb fits the profile to a T.

Now 35, Emilio Pagán was sensational after returning from a hamstring injury in July, pitching to a 1.88 ERA with 34 strikeouts and only five walks in his final 28 ⅔ innings. The downside is the same as it's always been: Pagán is exceptionally home run prone (career 1.51 HR/9), which is a bad trait for a late-inning reliever who pitches almost exclusively in close games. His fastball remains firm, though, and his splitter is an elite swing-and-miss pitch that allows him to neutralize righties and lefties. As long as you're willing to live with the home run risk, Pagán remains a capable high-leverage reliever, one who is not out of place pitching important innings for a contending team.

Platoon DHs are not the hottest commodity, but Joc Pederson fills the role about as well as anyone in the game. He's a left-handed hitter, so he's on the heavy side of the platoon, and he authored a .245/.338/.496 line with terrific ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) against righties. If you must play him in the field, Pederson can stand in right field or at first base for about six innings before being subbed out for a defensive replacement. He's essentially a bat-only player, though. Pederson will turn 35 in April and he's still a powerful and productive hitter against righties and an elite clubhouse vibes dude.

Naturally, with favorites dominating the day, it wasn't a banner showing from us in last week's column. That said, we did correctly pinpoint New England as a prime upset candidate to Green Bay, so we'll take the win when we can get it.

With favorites finding so much success last week, however, it should heighten their concern heading into Week 10, as the pendulum could swing in the other direction to even things up. And there are several games to choose from this weekend for potential upsets, including a "Sunday Night Football" showdown between two AFC North rivals. So, let's get right to it and identify five favorites who are on upset alert.

The last time these two NFC East rivals faced one another, it was a calamity that resulted in a 27-27 tie. That said, I do think Washington is catching New York at the right time in this Thursday night matchup to begin Week 10.

Giants starter J.J. McCarthy was in and out of the lineup last week after suffering a hip pointer injury against the Eagles, but is expected to play in this game. Before going down, McCarthy seemed more like his Minnesota self than the quarterback who completed 20-of-28 in a win over the Texans before their bye. McCarthy threw for 127 yards on 12-of-19 passing in the win over Philly, with his yards per attempt (6.7) taking a noticeable dip from his first two appearances. He also took five sacks.

If that continues on Thursday against a Commanders defense that is allowing just 15.0 points per game over the past two games, Washington's offense may not have to do too much heavy lifting. Meanwhile, Jayden Daniels has largely had success against New York, coming into this game with a 3-0-1 record against his division foe. He's also totaled five touchdowns and zero turnovers in those games. Daniels has largely protected the ball this season as well and has yet to throw an interception.

So, the recipe for Washington here is for Daniels to keep a clean sheet in the turnover margin, and for McCarthy to come back down to earth.

Maybe a trip across the Atlantic snaps the Patriots back into form after an abysmal loss to the Packers at home in Week 9. One of the biggest issues for New England's offense this season has been turnovers, committing one on 19.4% of drives. While that's hardly going to instill much confidence in anyone backing the Patriots in Week 10, it is worth noting that Detroit hasn't exactly been known to create turnovers on defense. Entering this international game in Germany, the Lions have eight turnovers this season, which is tied for the fourth-fewest in the NFL. When you compare that to Green Bay's 19 total turnovers (second-best), the Patriots should get some reprieve in that department.

Meanwhile, Jared Goff hasn't looked as lights-out as he did over the first five games of the season when he was an early MVP candidate. Even amid this winning streak, Goff's numbers have dipped.

He's still playing at a high level, but it's not otherworldly, which could help New England's defense -- particularly the secondary -- put together a bounce-back performance.

Minnesota has the disadvantage of being on the road against a division rival and being on a short week after playing on Monday night, but they do get a huge boost on offense for this game. Before Tuesday's trade deadline, the Vikings pulled off a trade to acquire Kirk Cousins from the Raiders, which should elevate the offense to a more respectable level.

Coming into the week and pre-Cousins, Minnesota ranks 31st in passing yards per game (160.8) and is tied with the winless Chargers for the fewest offensive touchdowns (11) in the NFL this season. Despite all that, they're 6-2, which is thanks to their top-flight defense. Now that they have an offense that can not only complement them, but sustain drives to give them more rest on the sideline, Minnesota should be taken more seriously.

The defense will have its hands full against Green Bay's prolific passing attack, but they do have the personnel to contain them. That's especially true in the aftermath of Josh Jacobs (broken finger) being ruled out for this game, further limiting an already anemic ground game.

The Packers have also struggled in this spot. The club is 1-5 in its past six games against division opponents (including playoffs) and are 1-8 in its last nine games against teams entering the matchup four or more games over .500.

With the shot in the arm on offense with Cousins' arrival, the Vikings are live at Lambeau.

Carolina is in the midst of a three-game losing streak, which has brought Bryce Young's play into focus. Over the last three games, the Panthers quarterback has averaged 216 passing yards per game, has five passing touchdowns and four interceptions. While that's not great, context is key. Young and the Panthers have squared off against the Buccaneers, Packers (road), and Broncos during the skid, all of which are among the top defenses in the league right now. New Orleans is not that.

The Saints secondary has allowed 7.3 yards per attempt so far this season (tied for the fifth-highest in the league) along with a 99.5 passer rating allowed (seventh-highest). Meanwhile, Young was solid last week, albeit in defeat. He completed 71.7% of his throws for 276 yards, three touchdowns and a pick. That output should hold up against a weaker defense in New Orleans and should help propel them to snap the losing streak.

That's especially true considering the Saints haven't been a strong team at home so far in 2026. At the Superdome, they are 1-4 and have yet to cover (0-5 ATS).

Whoever constructed the schedule this year did the Bengals dirty for this Week 10 matchup. Not only are they returning from an international game in Madrid last week, but they are hosting a Steelers club that was on the bye in Week 9. That's a massive rest disadvantage for Cincinnati, which could rear its head in this matchup.

So far, Joe Burrow has been the talk of the NFL as he's leaped to the top of the MVP conversation after a sensational run over the Bengals' four-game winning streak. He has the offense averaging over 35 points per game and has 18 total touchdowns with a 132.0 passer rating. While those are video-game-like numbers, the competition he's been slicing up hasn't exactly been the Legion of Boom. Over the streak, Cincinnati has beaten up on the Dolphins, Ravens (no Lamar Jackson), Titans and Falcons.

The Steelers pose a much tougher challenge, especially on defense. Pittsburgh is tied for the fifth-lowest yards per play average (5.0), tied for the fourth-lowest points per game allowed (18.0), and tied for the eighth-lowest passer rating allowed (83.3).

Since 2020, the Steelers have also won and covered in each of their six games coming off the bye.

#2637. Thunder trade grades: OKC swipes promising young wing Nique Clifford from the rebuilding Kings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We have our first trade of the 2026-27 NBA season, and it's a somewhat familiar one. The Oklahoma City Thunder are acquiring guard Nique Clifford from the Sacramento Kings, according to ESPN, reversing a trade that occurred during the 2025 NBA Draft. The Thunder, using a pick acquired from the Los Angeles Clippers, were on the clock at No. 24 overall, but the Kings moved into that slot to select Clifford. Now, a bit more than a year later, Clifford lands with the team whose hat he wore on draft night.

Trades this early in an NBA season are rare. Until Dec. 15, around 29% of the league is still technically untradeable because of contracts signed over the summer. However, the Oklahoma City Thunder have been ravaged by injuries so far this season. They initially planned to use their open roster spot to sign former first-round pick Ochai Agbaji, but changed course before doing so as their health issues worsened. Instead, they signed Dalen Terry to a non-guaranteed deal; they will now presumably waive him in order to take a swing on Sacramento's promising youngster. With the season's first trade done, let's grade it for both sides.

One of the advantages of working with the enormous draft surplus Oklahoma City has had since it traded Paul George to the Clippers is that it allows the Thunder to be opportunistic. Think of last February, when they stole Jared McCain from the Philadelphia 76ers for a single first-round pick. McCain was struggling through such a tough year that few teams could have afforded the risk of giving up a first-rounder for him. The Thunder obviously could, and in doing so, they got a key performer with two and a half years of cheap cost control remaining.

The thinking here is somewhat similar. The Thunder have so many second-round picks that they wouldn't miss two of them. The Kings, like the 76ers, decided they were ready to cut bait on a recent first-round pick who had shown promise far earlier than most teams would have, so the Thunder, with access to a roster spot through Terry's non-guaranteed deal and second-round picks to spare, jumped at the chance to take a swing on yet another valuable asset with several years of cost control.

Is Clifford going to be as helpful for Oklahoma City as McCain? Probably not, but there's plenty of reason to believe he can help this depleted version of the Thunder. Clifford averaged just under 13 points, five rebounds and four assists in March and April last year for a Kings team that may have been terrible, but wasn't actively trying to lose like many of its contemporaries.

His emergence as a genuine NBA Draft prospect came in his last two collegiate seasons, when he improved as a 3-point shooter playing at Colorado State. That shooting, coupled with his all-around production and bothersome 6-foot-8 wingspan as a defender, made him a promising role player prospect. Clifford does a little bit of everything. If the shots are falling, pretty much anyone could use a high-IQ, high-motor, ball-handling wing who rebounds well for his position.

This is, again, a flyer. We might find out that the Kings are giving up on him because they think he's a lemon. Think of their decision to dump Devin Carter two years after picking him in the lottery. Sometimes teams just know. Of course, the Kings are hardly the best evaluators of their own talent. See: Haliburton, Tyrese. We can't give the Thunder a straight "A" here because we've only ever seen Clifford as a productive player at the end of a single regular season for a terrible team. For all we know, the end of last season was a March mirage for Clifford. Plenty of teams fall for those.

But the cost here, for Oklahoma City's purposes, effectively amounts to loose change it found between its couch cushions. The upside is a real rotation player it can afford for several years. That's the definition of "low risk, high reward.

When the Kings drafted Clifford, he was joining a version of the team that still harbored (admittedly delusional) visions of remaining competitive. After last season, the plan changed. The Kings are moving into a rebuild now, and everything Sacramento does is geared toward the development of No. 7 overall pick Darius Acuff Jr., who currently has the second-highest rookie usage rate in NBA history. After averaging 25 minutes per game last season, Clifford has played just 50 through eight games this season. He hasn't made his shots in that small sample, which is a critical trait for anyone attempting to play off of Acuff.

Now, we're in the post-tanking NBA. In the past, we could have more fully admonished the Kings for playing veterans who won't be a part of their future, like Zach LaVine and Malik Monk, while plastering Clifford to the bench. Sacramento wants to avoid the relegation zone, so that makes a bit more sense now than it might have in the past. Couple that with the emergence of second-round pick Emanuel Sharp and former undrafted free agent Leaky Black as parts of the rotation and the impending return of Keegan Murray from a sprained ankle, and suddenly there just weren't many perimeter minutes available in Sacramento.

That all sounds fine on paper, but the NBA isn't a paper league. Players get hurt. Players get traded. Circumstances change. This was not something that needed to get settled in November of Clifford's second season. Even the Sixers waited until February to move McCain a season ago. Inevitably, there would have been more opportunities for the Kings to see what they had in Clifford as part of the Acuff-centric version of the team had they simply waited for those opportunities to arise. Sacramento simply has not earned the benefit of the doubt a team would need to justify giving up on a young player who has shown actual promise this quickly.

If this was a financially driven decision, it was still a hasty one. The Kings still had a year before they needed to make a decision on his fourth-year option. They already dropped below the luxury tax by waiving and stretching DeMar DeRozan, and there is not an immediately apparent benefit to saving another $3.3 million or so underneath it. Perhaps one will present itself later, but moving a player at this price point is typically easy enough that the Kings didn't have to rush this.

If this is a low-risk, high-reward trade for the Thunder, it's the opposite for the Kings. Best-case scenario, they're right about Clifford's value... and they get two second-round picks for someone they themselves decided was worth trading up to No. 24 to get. Not a great look for the organization. If they're wrong about Clifford and the Thunder manage to turn him into a real player as they do for almost everyone they acquire, they not only lose out on a valuable, cost-controlled asset, but become an object of ridicule for what feels like the hundredth time in the past two decades.

Last year's NBA Finals was a battle between Sacramento's former point guard (De'Aaron Fox and the San Antonio Spurs) and its former coach (Mike Brown and the New York Knicks). The 2025 Finals were nearly won by Haliburton, another former Kings point guard, and the 2023 Finals were won by Michael Malone, another former Kings coach. It's obviously unlikely that the Thunder manage to rally past all of these injuries and make it back to the Finals, and it's probably less likely that Clifford is the single reason why that would happen, but if he turns out to be a real part of a resurgent Thunder team, that will mark yet another humiliation for this Kings organization.

#2635. Winning trophies at Bayern was a "weight off the shoulders" for Harry Kane

Harry Kane has revealed that winning silverware at Bayern Munich was a big relief to him in terms of his career and confidence.

"Once I won the first trophy at Bayern, it was a weight off the shoulders in terms of a talking point in interviews and press conferences.

“It helped me relax and feel more free without thinking too much and having that extra pressure,” he said at England's press meeting this afternoon.

"It was tough in those moments when you feel you're performing well and putting up great numbers but not winning the team trophies which is ultimately what you're playing for.

“My situation was quite unique in that sense, I don't know if there has been another player like that who hasn't won for so long,” the striker said upon reflection.

Regardless, having claimed two Bundesliga titles, a DFB-Pokal and now a Ballon d'Or, Kane hopes he's only getting his collection started.

I'm in a sweet spot of my career where I've won many trophies in the last couple of years and hopefully loads more to go.

“Hopefully by the end of my career, I'll have 20+ trophies and those first 10 years might not be spoken about as much,” he added.

#2634. Buyer Beware: 5 NFL deadline trades that could become the next Sauce Gardner bust

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As in-season trades become all the more prevalent in the NFL, the risk of overspending also rises. That was most clear in 2025 when the Indianapolis Colts made perhaps the most regrettable trade in league history by sending two first-round picks to the New York Jets in exchange for cornerback Sauce Gardner. Those draft picks are golden with the Colts entering a deep rebuild, while Gardner has played the worst football of his career since landing in Indianapolis.

When teams pulled off 18 deals ahead of the 2026 trade deadline, they did so hoping to avoid the disaster that was the Colts' acquisition of Gardner. Chances are high that none of this year's trades will be as lopsided as that one, but it is far too soon to rule it out.

Only one transaction this year included two first-round picks, and it is already paying dividends for the purchasing side. And only one other included a single first-rounder. That does not mean that all of the teams involved are out of the woods just yet, though.

Here are the 2026 in-season trades with the greatest potential to go down as busts.

The trade that most resembles the infamous Sauce Gardner deal is the one that moved Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears. The Tennessee Titans secured two first-round picks in the swap. There will always be long-term risks (most notably regarding injury), but Simmons has already delivered, in a small sample size, everything the Bears could have asked of him. The superstar defensive tackle notched a sack and pass breakup in both of his first two games and logged an additional tackle for loss in his debut and elevated the entire unit around him in the process. It is far too soon to close the book on this trade, but all indications suggest it is a slam dunk for the Super Bowl-contending Bears.

Many elements of the Jordan Davis trade make sense for the Jacksonville Jaguars as they pursue the first Super Bowl in franchise history. The most obvious of them is that Davis fills an immediate need that arose when DaVon Hamilton went down with a season-ending torn quad muscle. But there is a great deal of inherent risk that comes with moving a 2027 first-round pick and 2029 second-rounder to land him. It is an all-in move that will either pay tremendous dividends or go down as an overpay. There is very little middle ground when it comes to these kinds of blockbuster trades.

Davis has to be a difference-maker from the jump. The Jaguars are in play for the AFC's No. 1 seed and will battle until season's end to secure it. More importantly, this trade will be judged in the context of what Davis delivers in the postseason. Anything short of a Super Bowl run is suddenly a disappointment, and Davis needs to play a major role in their championship pursuit.

From a run-stopping standpoint, Davis should give the Jaguars everything they lost from Hamilton and more. For the price they paid, it would be preferable if Davis were more of a threat as a pass rusher, however. He has never logged more than 4.5 sacks in a season. If offenses have to take blockers away from other players to account for him, then perhaps the added pocket disruption from the edges will make up for his lack of havoc creation.

The 2023 Biletnikoff Award winner is already a bust of a No. 4 overall draft pick. Will his trade from the Arizona Cardinals to the Houston Texans be a bust, too? Unless Marvin Harrison Jr.'s new team can tap back into the production that made him a promising rookie two years ago, the investment of a second-round pick to acquire him will go down as a steep price to pay for no more than a tertiary option in a deep receiving corps.

With time, Harrison's reunion with his college quarterback, C.J. Stroud, may prove fruitful. It would be unfair to ask those two to hit the ground running as a prolific tandem considering their time apart and the amount of time it takes to settle into a new system, but over the long term (and there is a long term here with Harrison under contract through 2027 and potentially into 2028) it is a reasonable expectation. Harrison is still a talented player, and Stroud is rounding into a standout franchise quarterback this season. On paper, those two things should mesh well.

There are warning signs about Harrison's future as a viable NFL starter, though, most notably in the form of his questionable effort in Arizona. And while he does have a touchdown already in Houston, he has not caught more than three passes in a game since joining the Texans and has only run 29 routes over three games. All three of his appearances came off the bench, too.

The modest playing time could be a result of Houston easing him into action until he gets a firm grasp on the playbook and rebuilds his connection with Stroud, but it may also indicate that he is not a top option in what has quickly become a crowded wide receiver group. Stroud has to battle each of these players for targets:

That is not to mention tight end Dalton Schultz, who leads all Texans with 47 targets on the season.

If it pans out, the Kirk Cousins move could be the most impactful in-season trade of them all and spark a Super Bowl run for the Minnesota Vikings. His potential to elevate the offense and maximize the team's potential with its otherworldly defense is real. But there is also a risk that Cousins cannot replicate what he did with the Las Vegas Raiders over the first half of the season, and the Vikings give up a third-round pick for a lateral move at quarterback rather than an upgrade over Kyler Murray.

Cousins was rejuvenated in Sin City and played his best version of football since his first stint in Minnesota. He is even on pace to flirt with the first 40-touchdown season of his career. The 38-year-old who fell out of favor with the Atlanta Falcons turned himself back into a starter and a highly productive one at that. But that came in an immensely quarterback-friendly system that coach Klint Kubiak has proven can turn middle-of-the-road passers into standouts. What happens when he leaves that scheme?

The last time Cousins played for Kevin O'Connell, he made the Pro Bowl. His fit in the Vikings' offense may be just as ideal as the one he displayed in Las Vegas. The numbers, in fact, suggest it could be even better.

But the last time Cousins played for the Minnesota Timberwolves was when he was 35, before he tore his Achilles. This is a different quarterback than the one who won 13 games in his last 17-game season in 2022.

The Dallas Cowboys have only gotten one game of full-strength Joey Porter Jr. despite trading for him all the way back on Oct. 1. He did not record a statistic in that debut. Since then, Porter missed a game due to illness, missed another with an ankle injury, and played through the ankle issue in two other games. It remains to be seen whether he will return to the lineup in Week 10 after he missed last week's win over the Indianapolis Colts.

When he is on the field, Porter is a lockdown cornerback. He allowed no better than a minuscule 47.9 passer rating in any of his first three games with the Cowboys across 10 targets. He still has permitted just one touchdown in his career and has gone 1,570 coverage snaps since then, according to Next Gen Stats. But if he cannot stay in the lineup, he will not be worth the 2028 second-round pick and 2027 sixth-rounder the Cowboys gave up to acquire him from the Pittsburgh Steelers. Especially if he leaves in free agency.

That is the next major question in this marriage between Porter and Dallas. Will he stick around beyond this year? The Steelers were unwilling to meet his reported demands to make him one of the highest-paid cornerbacks in the NFL, and Jerry Jones does not exactly have a history of paying players what they ask for, either. This could turn out to be a one-year rental for a player who has already missed time.

Plus, it is not like the Cowboys' defense at large has taken any major steps forward since Porter joined the unit. The NFL's third-worst group in yards allowed per game remains a stain on what would otherwise be a post-season caliber roster, with its star-studded offense and all.

Similar to the Porter trade, the deal that sent Quenton Nelson from the Indianapolis Colts to the Seattle Seahawks has a cloud of uncertainty hanging over it because of a health issue. Nelson underwent a minor procedure to clean up cartilage fragments in his knee and is labeled as week-to-week. He will not play in Week 10 but has also not landed on injured reserve, which indicates he could be back by early December.

Seattle gave up a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to land Nelson on Oct. 27 and thus paid a fairly modest price for one of the top interior offensive linemen of the 2020s. Still, it will only be worth the investment if Nelson gets and stays healthy and upgrades a dormant running game. Before his knee surgery, he did not bring tangible improvement to the ground attack. The Seahawks managed 81 yards in his debut (their second-lowest total of the season) and rushed for a modest 3.6 yards per carry in a slugfest last week.

Nelson's health and ongoing rushing issues have already knocked a few points off the Seahawks' value in what initially seemed like a home-run trade. There is still plenty of time to salvage it, and if he re-signs in free agency, that would go a long way in making the deal age phenomenally. But there is an outcome in which Nelson plays below full strength for most of the year and then leaves in the offseason. In the aggregate, Seattle would be out at least one draft pick (potentially two depending on the compensatory formula) and an All-Pro guard in that case.

#2633. NHL Power Rankings: New Jersey Devils looking scary after Connor Hellebuyck trade

We're in the throes of spooky season, and fittingly, the New Jersey Devils just got a lot scarier with the acquisition of superstar goaltender Connor Hellebuyck.

One of the best goaltenders in the world, Hellebuyck fills the biggest need on the Devils roster. With him in between the pipes and an electrifying group of forwards, New Jersey will be a force in the Eastern Conference.

Don't take my word for it. Just look at what the Devils did Tuesday against the Dallas Stars. In his first start with the team, Hellebuyck stopped 17 of the 18 shots he faced -- allowing one goal on 2.04 expected goals against -- in a 5-1 victory.

Nico Hischier, Jack Hughes and Luke Hughes each had multi-point nights as the Devils took full advantage of the chances they created against a stout Dallas team. This type of game has to be exactly what general manager Sunny Mehta envisioned when he swung the deal for Hellebuyck.

Moving forward, the Devils will be burdened with the pressure that comes along with being a bona fide Cup contender. For a franchise that's fallen short of expectations a few times lately, that can be a scary prospect, and it inspired a special Halloween edition of the NHL Power Rankings in which I highlight the scariest thing about each team.

#2632. Jayson Tatum won't give air to Jaylen Brown drama ahead of Celtics-Sixers game: 'Another game on the schedule'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MILWAUKEE -- Jayson Tatum downplayed Tuesday's showdown between the Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers, which will be the first time that he and former teammate Jaylen Brown will face each other as opponents.

"It's another game on the schedule. It's the Celtics versus the Sixers. In the words of Brad Stevens, they all count as one," Tatum said after putting up 21 points, four rebounds and six assists in a 117-97 win over the Milwaukee Bucks. "This one counted as one. Go get ready for Tuesday. It's a really good team, obviously. Incredible group, great coaching staff, they've been playing really well. So from that standpoint it's gonna be fun. But it's nothing more than Celtics versus Sixers."

Tatum and Brown spent nine seasons together, and led the Celtics to the 2024 championship -- the historic franchise's first since 2008 and record-setting 18th overall -- before the latter was traded to Philadelphia this summer in a blockbuster deal that brought Paul George to Boston.

Much has been made about Tatum and Brown's relationship, or lack thereof, particularly over the last few weeks.

Late last month, Tatum shared his recollection of the trade in an episode of his documentary series, "Summer of Jayson." "I was just as much caught off guard as the rest of the world," he said. In the comment section of the clip online, Brown called "cap."

Shortly after, Tatum tried to shut down any drama by pointing to all that they had accomplished together. "This ain't no f---in' Shaq and Kobe, there's no beef," Tatum said. "It's not about that. It should be more praise, and I understand that don't necessarily sell. Drama gets clicks and views, but I'm not really — that's not my thing."

Brown, on the other hand, played into the drama a few days later. "There's no beef," Brown said. "Jayson comes from a wonderful family. We've accomplished some great things. He's a hell of a basketball player. He's got a great PR team. It's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chop. And some gravy. He should stay ready at all times."

Now, as the first meeting between the former teammates arrives, both have tried to keep the focus on basketball.

"It's nothing to talk about. I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said after the 76ers secured a 127-121 win over the Chicago Bulls on Sunday. "Just playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win, so it's nothing to talk about. Just check the ball up. ... "We'll see how I feel when we get out there, but as of now, I got no emotion towards anything. So I'm just ready to go."

When Tatum asked if he would have a conversation with Brown on Tuesday, his response was a simple "I'm not able to tell the future," before adding that he had "no idea" if any such conversation would have to wait until after the season.

"I just know that it's the Celtics versus the Sixers. Just go out there and do my job and try to get another win," Tatum said. "Get through that, got a game on Wednesday. It's a long season. We got 72 games left. That's just the focus right now."

As for the actual basketball, both players and teams are off to terrific starts. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and four assists on 47.7% shooting, including 39.2% from 3-point range, for the 9-2 Sixers, who sit atop the Eastern Conference. Tatum, meanwhile, is at 27.1 points, six rebounds and 7.8 assists for the 8-2 Celtics, who are alone in second.

#2631. MLB free agency: Six international players to know for the 2026-27 offseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball's free agency period opened earlier this week and teams are now clear to pursue any roster upgrades they deem necessary. That includes players coming over from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league, South Korea's Korea Baseball Organization, and Taiwan's Chinese Professional Baseball League. Those are high-level leagues that have sent many impact players MLB's way over the years.

Look no farther than the Dodgers to see how important international talent can be to a club. The Dodgers employed four different former NPB and KBO players this past season, including two-way star Shohei Ohtani, ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and starter Roki Sasaki. Ohtani was signed as an MLB free agent, but the others went to the Dodgers through the posting system.

Per the posting agreement with MLB, posted NPB and CPBL players get a 45-day window to negotiate and sign with an MLB team. KBO players get a 30-day window. Players who do not sign during that posting window return to their previous team in NPB, CPBL, or KBO. The MLB team that signs a posted player pays a fee to the player's former NPB, CPBL, or KBO team.

$5M plus 17.5% of contract value over $25M

$9.375M plus 15% of contract value over $50M

For example, the White Sox paid Munetaka Murakami's former team, the Yakult Swallows, a $6.575 million posting fee on his $34 million contract last offseason. That's $5 million on the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the remaining $9 million, which is $1.575 million. The $5 million plus $1.575 million equals the $6.575 million posting fee paid to the Swallows.

Unlike last lockout, MLB will not be pausing the signing window during the expected lockout, according to The Athletic. In other words, if owners lock players out on Dec. 1 as expected, that date will essentially serve as the same deadline for already posted NPB players unless the lockout ends before their 45-day window expires.

There are no superstar-caliber players like Ohtani or Yamamoto available in this winter's international free agent crop. There are, however, several interesting players who can improve an MLB roster in 2027. Here are the six best NPB, CPBL, and KBO players to know this offseason.

Japan's Triple Crown winner hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. He has a similar skill set to Murakami but is not exactly Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games in 2026 around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll. The Hanshin Tigers officially posted Sato on Nov. 1.

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Taira was officially posted on Nov. 1.

A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Itoh on Nov. 1.

Roh has an unusual agreement with the Hanwha Eagles. He signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and roughly $23 million), and as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him for MLB teams this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the Eagles to finish his career when his big-league stint is over. This past season, Roh, 26 in November, authored a .283/.360/.505 batting line with 29 home runs. He has real right-handed power and a good approach at the plate. There are concerns about his propensity to swing and miss as well as his arm at the hot corner. The Eagles formally posted Roh on Nov. 1.

The Seibu Lions posted Takahashi last offseason, but he was unable to find a contract to his liking, so he returned to Japan for another season and threw 148 innings with a 2.64 ERA. Takahashi, 30 in February, is an international free agent now, meaning he does not have to be posted and can instead negotiate at his own pace. More of a ground ball pitcher than a bat-misser, Takahashi sits in the 91-95 mph range with his fastball and has two good secondary pitches in his slider and splitter. He also throws a cutter and curveball. Takahashi is considered a potential innings guy for the back of an MLB rotation.

Tseng pitched for Chinese Taipei in the World Baseball Classic in 2023 and 2026 and he has been one of the CPBL's top relievers the last few years. In 2026, he saved 25 games with a 1.80 ERA and 65 strikeouts in 52 ⅓ innings. Tseng's fastball typically sits in the mid-90s and has run as high as 100 mph in the past, though it has been a few years. His go-to secondary pitch is a breaking ball that needs improvement for Tseng to carve out an MLB career as more than a middle reliever.

#2630. It wouldn't shock me if ... NFL Week 10: Fernando Mendoza struggles in first start, new Chiefs WR dominates

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Nine weeks and the trade deadline are now in our rearview mirror. From here on out, it's all gas no brakes through the second half of the regular season as we rocket towards the playoffs down the road to Super Bowl LXI. Of course, plenty will happen between now and when we kick off that championship match from SoFi Stadium, and we'll keep marching on with Week 10 on deck.

As always, unexpected storylines develop over the course of the season and in a given week, and we try to pinpoint some of them for you here before they arrive.

Last week, we highlighted a bounce-back performance from Bijan Robinson, who had 147 scrimmage yards in a loss to Cincinnati in Madrid. While he didn't commit multiple turnovers, we also put you on the scent of Jayden Daniels -- who fumbled -- being a little loose with the football, along with Jonah Coleman continuing to play well enough to soften Denver's need to acquire a back at the deadline.

We'll look to carry that momentum into this week. Below, you can find five storylines and/or individual performances we wouldn't be shocked to see happen in Week 10.

All NFL odds courtesy of DraftKings Sportsbook.

Rather quietly, Zach Charbonnet has looked good in his return from his ACL tear last January. He's played in two games for Seattle and is quickly taking over the backfield.

After a modest six carries in his first game back in Week 8, Charbonnet dominated the backfield touches in Week 9. The veteran back had 16 carries in the win over Arizona, well above Jadarian Price's 9 carries. On top of getting the lion's share of work, Charbonnet is proving to simply be the better back. He's averaging 4.5 yards per carry, far better than Price's 3.7 yards per carry on the season and 2.8 yards per carry since returning from IR in Week 8.

Given the current trajectory of both players, it wouldn't shock me to see Charbonnet continue to see the bulk of the touches out of the backfield. If he does, he has a chance to put together his best game so far: the Raiders are allowing 5.0 yards per carry this season, which is tied for the most in the NFL.

In fact, Charbonnet is liable to record just the third 100-yard rushing game of his career in this matchup.

Gambling nugget to note: Zach Charbonnet's rushing yards total for Week 10 is 60.5 (-113 to the Over).

Josh Downs was one of the notable names to be moved on deadline day, and the former Colts receiver suddenly finds himself in NFL nirvana. Not only was his trade request granted, but he was traded to the Kansas City Chiefs, where Patrick Mahomes will be his quarterback. Judging by his immediate reaction to the trade on social media, Downs is clearly happy with how things turned out.

I expect the Chiefs to see immediate returns from this move, as Downs fits how the offense has run this season perfectly. More than in any other season of his career, Mahomes and the Chiefs have primarily worked the short passing game, as his 5.6 air yards per attempt highlights. Downs is an elite separator. His 3.2 average yards of separation and +24 yards after the catch over expectation are 24th and tied for 24th among 72 qualified receivers, according to NFL Pro. Mahomes will quickly realize and exploit that ability.

Kansas City has desperately been looking for an answer at receiver as the position group is averaging just 117.5 receiving yards per game this season. Not only does that rank 28th in the NFL this season, but it's the fewest in the Mahomes era. Downs may change that overnight.

Atlanta is coming off a loss to the Bengals in Madrid, where the Cincinnati receivers ran wild. While Ja'Marr Chase is in a class of his own, I do believe Downs can have loads of success against this secondary that also just traded away star safety Jessie Bates.

Finally paired with a quarterback that can get him the football, Downs makes his presence felt early for Kansas City.

Gambling nugget to note: Josh Downs' receiving yard total for Week 10 is 30.5 (-109 to the Over).

The Fernando Mendoza era is about to begin in Las Vegas. The No. 1 overall pick is slated to make his first career start on Sunday, after the Raiders traded Kirk Cousins (who started the first nine games of the season) to the Minnesota Vikings before Tuesday's deadline.

While anticipation is building for a full look at Mendoza in the NFL, this isn't exactly the softest landing spot for him. The Indiana product will have the luxury of being at home, but at the same time will have the tall task of facing the Seattle Seahawks defense.

The unit is allowing just 244.2 total yards of offense per game, including 155.1 passing yards allowed per game. Both are the fewest in the NFL. On top of that, their 4.1 total yards per play allowed is the lowest by any team through nine games since the 2023 Ravens. They're also surrendering the fewest 20-yard plays (17) through nine games since the 2008 Steelers.

Facing the defending Super Bowl champs presents a tough challenge for Mendoza to come out of the gate firing in his first start. In fact, he's the first quarterback taken No. 1 overall to face the defending champions in his first career start. The five previous first-round rookie quarterbacks to debut against the reigning champs have all lost.

Meanwhile, No. 1 pick quarterbacks are 1-15-1 in their first career starts since 2003. Given that history, it's not worth hitting the panic button even if Mendoza does struggle.

Gambling nugget to note: Fernando Mendoza is -156 to throw an interception in Week 10.

Coming into Week 10, Joe Burrow is the odds-on favorite to win the NFL MVP award at +190. He's followed by Josh Allen, who has +250 odds to win the award for the second time in his career. After that, however, is Brock Purdy at +425. By the end of Week 10, however, it's plausible that Purdy ascends to the top of these odds as the new favorite to win the award.

As I've written about elsewhere this week, I think there's a possibility the Steelers cool down Joe Burrow on "Sunday Night Football." To his credit, Burrow has put up otherworldly numbers, but it's come against subpar competition. He faces a much tougher task against Pittsburgh, who is top five in the NFL in yards per play allowed and points per game allowed. The defense is also tied for the eighth-lowest passer rating allowed. Coming off of their bye, while Cincinnati returns from a game in Spain, there's the potential for him to post a dud in primetime, which will ding his odds.

Meanwhile, Purdy gets an advantageous matchup himself as he and the 49ers will roll into AT&T Stadium to face the Cowboys. Dallas is giving up the third-most total yards per game in the NFL and the third-most yards per play. Moreover, they're giving up 26.2 points per game (bottom 10 in the NFL), opponents are converting 48.31% of their third-down opportunities (highest), and a 99.1 passer rating (eighth-highest).

Purdy is top-three in the NFL in completion percentage, yards per attempt, and passer rating this season and has a history of dominating against the Cowboys. For his career, the 49ers QB is 3-0 against Dallas, averaging 9.2 yards per attempt and a 118.4 passer rating.

The stage is set for another monster outing. If he plays to that level, the MVP chatter surrounding him will only get louder.

Speaking of awards, Will Anderson Jr. is becoming the overwhelming favorite to win Defensive Player of the Year in 2026.

Currently, his odds to win DPOY are down to +150, with Fred Warner the next up behind him at +600. That's thanks to Anderson piling up 9.5 sacks, which are the most in the NFL through nine weeks and the second-most by a Texans player in the first eight games of a season (J.J. Watt with 105 in 2012). Anderson is one of the game's elite pass rushers, and I expect him to only bolster his case to win the award with what could be a career performance on Sunday against the Browns.

Cleveland is set to have Deshaun Watson after the veteran quarterback missed last week's loss to New Orleans after landing in concussion protocol. Despite missing a game, Watson still enters Week 10 with a league-high 33 sacks taken this season. Meanwhile, Shedeur Sanders was sacked five times last week. No matter who is under center for the Browns, they get sacked early and often, which is music to Anderson's ears.

The most sacks he's posted in a single game of his career is three, which he's done twice. The first came back in 2024 in a Week 6 game against the Patriots. The second was earlier this year, sacking Cam Ward three times in a Week 5 win over Tennessee. Against a beatable Browns offensive line, Anderson adds another three-sack game to his résumé.
