#2528. Naz Reid landing spots: Four NBA contenders that make sense if Hornets look to move sharp-shooting big man

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

You could argue that before this season, there was not a single role player in the NBA more beloved by his own fanbase than Naz Reid. Simply uttering his name, devoid of context, became a popular meme among the Minnesota Timberwolves faithful in recent years, and for good reason. The former undrafted free agent grew into a Sixth Man of the Year winner and one of the best shooting bigs in basketball during his seven-year run with the Timberwolves. Leaving the only team he had ever known this offseason has proven difficult thus far.

Reid, 27, is posting big raw numbers in his first season as a full-time starter with the Charlotte Hornets, but there are bigger concerns under the surface. After shooting just under 57% on 2-pointers in Minnesota, he is at around 44% with the Hornets and struggling to score efficiently near the basket. His defense has raised eyebrows as well, and after he was benched in an early game against the Detroit Pistons, Hornets coach Charles Lee said that Reid "didn't meet our standards in the first half, and at halftime we made the decision that he wouldn't play in the second half."

Reid, along with an unprotected 2033 first-round pick, was one of the centerpieces of Charlotte's return in trading star guard LaMelo Ball to Minnesota. The 4-7 Hornets have struggled mightily without Ball, posting the NBA's worst offensive rating this season despite having the league's best offense from early December forward last season. Injuries have played a big part in those struggles, but at this stage, Reid's role as a foundational Hornets player moving forward is already coming into question. Timberwolves beat writer Jon Krawczynski of The Athletic even said on his podcast that the chances of Reid getting traded again are "very high."

"The Hornets now are clearly in a period of transition, and they decided that LaMelo Ball was not going to be a part of the team that they believe can eventually get to real contender status," Krawczynski explained. "They made a decision with that core group that they were not good enough as constructed and so they had to take a step back, amass some assets and go forward. And what that also means is that, A, the fans are going to be upset because they finally had a fun season last year and now it is going sideways again, but B, the possibilities of Naz Reid getting traded again are very high. This is a roster that I think is going to change over quite a bit over the next couple of years as the Hornets look for the right combination of people to really vault into what they hope is contention."

Krawczynski did not specify a timetable, and we've certainly seen frustrating starts turn into fruitful long-term partnerships, but all of this underlines just how difficult things have been for Reid and the Hornets so far this season. Charlotte knew what it was doing by trading Ball. The idea was to take a step back now to take a bigger step forward later. If that's still the idea here, there should be plenty of teams with real interest in Reid, so let's identify a few possible landing spots for the sweet-shooting big man.

The Warriors traded for and eventually re-signed Kristaps Porziņģis because they need big men who can shoot in a lineup featuring both Draymond Green and, presumably, Jimmy Butler eventually. Al Horford can cover some of those minutes, but he's 40 and can only be expected to play so much. Fortunately, Green's ability to defend across the positional spectrum means the Warriors don't necessarily need their center-sized shooter to actually defend centers. If he's big, he rebounds and he shoots, he'll fit.

This is Reid to a T. With Green on the team to actually guard the most dangerous centers and the combination of Butler and Yaxel Lendeborg providing size on the wing, the Warriors are fairly well-equipped to minimize Reid's weaknesses. His strengths are exactly what the Warriors need; the not-currently-getting-paid Porziņģis takes Golden State most of the way there when it comes to salary matching (with only a smaller salary like Gui Santos or De'Anthony Melton needed to close the hard cap gap), and the Warriors control almost all of their own future draft capital, so they have the ammunition they'd need to satisfy the Hornets.

The big question here -- especially with Stephen Curry now set to miss around a month with an oblique abdominal tear -- is how eager the Warriors are to invest in their present. Before the season, the answer should have been a resounding "not at all." But Curry was playing like an MVP candidate before he got hurt, and the emergence of Lendeborg as the Rookie of the Year favorite has arguably changed the equation. While the Warriors (8-4) may not be able to justify an all-in trade, giving up, say, one unprotected pick to nab the 27-year-old Reid, who can be a part of their post-Curry future as well as their present, might be a satisfactory compromise.

The Pistons have reportedly had an eye on Reid ever since his anticipated 2025 free agency, but he wound up re-signing with Minnesota before the opening bell even rang. The appeal is obvious. Two of Detroit's three best players, Ausar Thompson and Jalen Duren, are non-shooters. Having a big man who can shoot theoretically helps offset that deficit, particularly in lineups featuring just one of those two. Detroit tried that very strategy this offseason in acquiring John Collins. The results have been mixed, with the Pistons faring far better in the minutes Collins sits than the ones he plays. Reid is better and younger.

The Pistons are enormously flexible in how they could construct a deal. They control all of their own first-round picks, and they have a fair bit of breathing room beneath the luxury tax. That breathing room evaporates next season, though, when Thompson's rookie extension kicks in. This is where the decision calculus gets harder. Duren and Cade Cunningham are already making market rate. Thompson will be next season, and Duncan Robinson has simply proven too indispensable to move on from. Paying all four of those players plus Reid would leave precious little flexibility to add the second ball-handler Detroit badly needs.

Maybe the Pistons feel they're good enough as is to win without one, or they could be prepared to trade someone else out of their core down the line if they feel compelled to seek out that needed ball-handling addition. The Trajan Langdon-led front office is now in its third season at the helm, yet it has not traded a single first-round pick amid Detroit's ascent. The Pistons have been cautious with buy-now moves. Maybe Reid is the sort of player they'd splurge for, but considering how well the Pistons are playing, they will likely be cautious in shaking things up too much.

Cleveland's starting five simply hasn't worked this season. The Cavaliers are getting crushed with their five starters on the floor, and the Jarrett Allen-Evan Mobley duo, a frequent target of the rumor mill, is losing its minutes together by over five points per 100 possessions. That duo has never generated the elite rebounding that double-big lineups are supposed to create, and while they do a good job of defending shots at the rim, they give up so many of them that they net out as a fairly underwhelming rim defense. Peyton Watson is struggling to fit in as a small forward, but lineups featuring him and just one of Mobley or Allen are faring far better.

Swapping one of the bigs out for Reid, essentially trading defense for shooting, recalibrates the team in ways that theoretically create a friendlier environment for Watson. The Hornets, still presumably looking for a long-term starter at center, would likely have some degree of interest in either Mobley or Allen. The question is which makes more sense in a trade like this.

The answer is probably Allen. He's older. He's worse. He's more traditionally a center than Mobley, whom Cleveland has historically been reluctant to move up from power forward. But the on-off data is pretty clear this season: Cleveland is playing better with Allen on the floor than it is with Mobley. If the Cavaliers are going to go with a single big, it might behoove them to stick with the one they know can be a center. Mobley's 30% max contract is going to prove limiting down the line, especially with Donovan Mitchell starting a 35% supermax deal next season. Mobley would almost certainly net more in a trade than Allen would, and Charlotte has the pick surplus to make a pretty compelling offer if it wants to.

If Mobley is available in any way, shape or form by February, offers will come in from several teams. Not many have a package that makes more immediate sense than one built around Reid and Charlotte's picks, which Cleveland could either keep or redirect for other assets. If Cleveland and Charlotte do engage on Reid talks, though, Allen is the far likelier Cavaliers big man to become a Hornet.

We can't fully judge the Raptors until we see an extended stretch with a healthy Kawhi Leonard, but thus far, Toronto's shooting weakness elsewhere has been as severe as expected. The Raptors rank 24th in 3-point attempt rate and 27th in 3-point percentage as of this writing. Like Golden State, Toronto is perfectly equipped to cover for Reid's deficiencies as a rim protector. There isn't a better trio of defensive forwards in the NBA than Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Collin Murray-Boyles, and Murray-Boyles already plays a reasonable amount of center.

The money would presumably be RJ Barrett's expiring contract. Losing his shot-creation would sting, but with a healthy Leonard, they should be covered in that respect. The question is draft compensation. The Raptors already gave up unprotected picks in 2031 and 2033 for Leonard, leaving their 2029 selection as their only tradable, unencumbered pick. They could move their 2027 pick as well, though it has swap rights attached to the Oklahoma City Thunder, limiting its appeal. A swap or two would probably be needed here to seal the deal, but Toronto probably has the chips to pull this off if it's motivated enough.

Reid would eat up Toronto's room beneath the luxury tax line next season, but with all of their core players locked in, that shouldn't be much of an issue. The Raptors haven't started their tax clock yet, so a year or two above that line (and still well below the dreaded second apron) seems a small price to pay for a genuine championship contender.

#2527. Now with an MVP, Pete Crow-Armstrong is on the path for an all-time great career. Where could he stack up?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The MVP winners were revealed Thursday evening and, unsurprisingly, the runaway unanimous winner in the National League was Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs.

Crow-Armstrong had an all-time great regular season, which is what the annual Baseball Writers' Association of America award honors. He hit .280/.372/.570 with stellar defense, led the league in home runs (tied with Kyle Schwarber) and massively upgraded his on-base skills. Now, just a few months shy of his 25th birthday, he has an MVP to his name.

So what's next? To answer that, we'll look backwards.

Since integration, only eight center fielders have posted at least 8.0 WAR in a season age-25 or younger: Willie Mays, Mickey Mantle, Willie Davis, César Cedeño, Ken Griffey Jr., Andruw Jones, Mike Trout and PCA. The only ones to top PCA's 9.8 were Mays, Mantle and Trout. If we went back to pre-integration, Tris Speaker and Ty Cobb were the only others who bested PCA here.

Willie Davis was an inconsistent hitter through his age-23 season but had flashed a nice power-speed combo. Sound familiar? That gaudy 8.4 WAR total in 1964, though, was driven largely by monster defensive metrics. Davis hit .294/.316/.413 (110 OPS+) with 23 doubles, seven triples, 12 home runs, 77 RBI, 91 runs and 42 steals. There's little doubt that PCA's 2026 season dwarfed this one overall, and Davis was far behind Mays (11.0) for the league lead in WAR.

For the rest of his career, Davis averaged 3.1 WAR per season, and though he had good years, he never reached 6.0 WAR again. The WAR figure was, again, mostly driven by defense. He had several good offensive seasons, but his only 20-homer season came in 1962 when he was 22, two years prior to his career year.

Davis' career probably looks a lot like PCA's apparent upside before his home run barrage in the first half of 2025. He racked up over 60 career WAR with a decent batting average, excellent defense and excellent baserunning.

With PCA reaching 30-30 last year and 40-40 this year, though, the bar has been raised.

César Cedeño followed up his 8.0 WAR season with a 7.4 season at age 22 and 5.8 at age 23. He was very good through age 29 and, in fact, the most statistically similar player through both ages 27 and 28 was Hall of Famer Carl Yastrzemski. Things fell apart after that. As a quick and easy way to illustrate it, Cedeño amassed 49.4 WAR through his age-29 season and only 3.6 in his final six years.

It's easier to remember that Andruw Jones' career unfolded in similar fashion because we witnessed it not too long ago and then discussed his Hall of Fame candidacy during his nine turns on the ballot before he finally made it in. In Jones' 12 Braves' season, he racked up 368 home runs, 1,117 RBI and 61 WAR while generally being considered the best defensive center fielder in baseball. Once he left, in time for his age-31 season, Jones accrued just 1.7 WAR in his last five seasons.

Through Jones' age-28 season, the most statistically similar players are Bryce Harper and Frank Robinson.

To compare these two to Crow-Armstrong, the argument would be that he'll continue to look like one of the best players in baseball -- even if taking steps backward from being the very best in the 2026 regular season -- before falling apart once he's around 30 years old.

Certainly possible, but given the adjustments he's already not only been willing to make at the plate, but eager to make, I'm just not seeing him all of a sudden hitting a wall. Sure, at some point he'll start losing speed and that'll affect his defensive range and baserunning, but why would the plate skills deteriorate all of a sudden?

Then again, few saw it coming with Jones.

All three of these players were on the path to having an argument as the best player in history before injuries derailed them in their 30s and left them as mere "all-time greats."

Through Mickey Mantle's age-30 season, he had 90.7 WAR. He averaged 121 games per year in his final six seasons, putting up 19.5 WAR. Through  Ken Griffey Jr.'s age-30 season, he had 76.2 WAR. He played 10 more seasons, but only amassed 7.6 more WAR. Through Mike Trout's age-27 season, he had 72.1 WAR (his top statistical similars were Mantle, Robinson and Griffey). We'll skip 2020 for obvious reasons, but since then he's averaged 90 games and 3.0 WAR per season.

Even with the drop-offs, it would be surprising to see Crow-Armstrong reach this level because it's surprising to see any player reach this lofty standard. In career WAR among center fielders, Mantle is fourth, Trout is fifth and Griffey is sixth. They trail only Cobb, Speaker and the guy we're going to discuss next. Joe DiMaggio is seventh.

Despite the lofty standard PCA set for himself in 2026, coming close to Willie Mays' career would be jaw-droppingly shocking, and that is absolutely not intended as a slight.

Mays has an argument as the greatest player in baseball history and he put himself in that discussion by being good at everything and doing it all with great longevity. From his age-23 to -35 seasons, he led the majors in WAR eight times, leading the NL an additional two times. His worst seasons in that timeframe were 7.6 and 7.8 WAR. In that span, he also led the league in runs twice, hits once, triples three times, home runs three times, stolen bases four times, average once, on-base percentage once, slugging percentage five times and OPS five times.

Mays even posted 5.2 WAR at age 39 and 6.3 at age 40. He led the NL with a .425 OBP when he was 40 years old! He hit .345/.411/.667 at age 23.

Mays' 156.2 career WAR ranks third among position players all-time behind two guys you might have heard of: Barry Bonds (162.8) and Babe Ruth (162.3).

I feel pretty strongly Pete Crow-Armstrong isn't headed for a run at this career and that's just fine.

The realistic long-term range for the 2026 National League MVP seems somewhere between Cedeño and Mantle. It's a wide variance of outcomes between those two, obviously, as well it should be when the player we discuss is only 24 years old. For his name to be mentioned among these at all is a testament to the year Crow-Armstrong just put together.

#2526. Grading every NFL team at the midway point: Chargers get an 'F,' three teams get solid 'A' grade

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We're just past the midway point of the NFL season, which means it's time to start thinking seriously about who has and has not met the expectations we set for them at the start of the year. Everyone came into the season with a different set of hopes, and everyone has had plenty of time to meet, exceed or fall short of them now that we have played nine weeks of football.

For some teams, whether they have done what was expected of them is fairly obvious: The Chargers have not, for example. For other teams, it's not so obvious: The entire NFC South would fit that description. But what about the rest of the teams in the league? How have they performed, and how would we grade them relative to what was expected of them entering the season?

That's why we're here. We're assigning letter grades to each team's performance through the midway point of the season. We broke down where each team stands, and why, below.

Dallas came into this season with high hopes but has instead disappointed. The Cowboys' defense remains a disaster, and the offense hasn't lived up to expectations. They've also blown a couple of games with poor situational football awareness. The only thing saving them from a worse grade is that the rest of the NFC East is bad enough that they're in second place and potentially in position to make a run at the playoffs.

The Giants could hardly have hoped for the start of the John Harbaugh era to go any better results-wise. They're in first place in the division despite having lost their starting quarterback in the second game of the season. Rookie Arvell Reese looks like a total monster. They have mostly won close games, so they might not be as good as their record indicates, but that doesn't matter when it comes to how they've performed relative to expectations.

The Eagles would have an F if not for Howie Roseman's smart pivot to selling off pieces at and around the trade deadline, which restocked the cupboard full of draft picks for the future. Philly is always smart about knowing when to pull the plug on a lost season, which is exactly what this year has been.

The Commanders weren't necessarily expected to be all that competitive in the NFC East this year, but the degree to which they've fallen behind the Giants and Cowboys is disappointing. The game management issues under Dan Quinn have also persisted, which contributes to this grade.

The Bears, like the rest of the NFC North, have to be happy with how their season has gone to date. The offense looks explosive, and the defense looks better after the addition of Jeffery Simmons. The only thing holding them back from getting a straight 'A' here is the surprising lack of run game efficiency, though Kyle Monangai's absence has contributed to that.

The Lions have one of the most explosive offenses in the league, with Jahmyr Gibbs, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams and Sam LaPorta combining with Jared Goff to light up scoreboards. The defense has even been playing better lately, albeit in light matchups. There have been some issues here and there (like the loss to the Panthers), but overall, things have gone quite well relative to expectations.

The Packers have to be thrilled with how their season has gone. Despite the absence of Micah Parsons, the defense has been excellent. Jordan Love is playing near an MVP level. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden look like superstars. The one thing holding them back from an 'A' is how they started the season, with a bad loss to Minnesota and the blowout against Atlanta. Otherwise, things have gone about as well as could be expected.

The Vikings' defense gets an A+++++, but the offense has been bad enough to knock the team down nearly a full letter grade despite Minnesota's 6-2 record. Here's hoping that Kirk Cousins can at least prop things up a bit for the rest of the season.

I can't justify giving any NFC South team anything other than a 'C' based on what they have done to date. They're all living down to relatively low expectations.

Same as above: I can't justify giving any NFC South team anything other than a 'C' based on what they have done to date. They're all living down to relatively low expectations.

I'll say it one more time: I can't justify giving any NFC South team anything other than a 'C' based on what they have done to date. They're all living down to relatively low expectations.

Sorry, this is the last time: I can't justify giving any NFC South team anything other than a 'C' based on what they have done to date. They're all living down to relatively low expectations.

The Cardinals have actually been better than anybody expected. They have three wins, and they've played a couple of other close games mixed in there. They do have five double-digit losses, though, so it's hard to give them a grade in the 'B' range. Things will also likely get worse the rest of the way, given their injury issues. That said, getting a second-round pick back for Marvin Harrison Jr. looks like a good deal.

The Super Team expectations were probably always a bit too high, but the Rams haven't come close for a variety of reasons. Whether it's injuries, Matthew Stafford's regression or even more injuries, you have to dock the Rams for not even being a surefire playoff team at the midpoint of the season. Being over .500 despite the injuries is mildly impressive, but not enough to give them a grade in the 'B' range.

The 49ers are a team that has overcome nearly as many injuries as the Rams have faced. It seems like as long as they have Kyle Shanahan, Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey and George Kittle, they are just going to keep humming. And Raheem Morris has the defense playing well despite its own injury issues. They've been great on both sides of the ball.

We initially had the Seahawks at a 'B-' grade, but then we remembered the odd loss to the Commanders in Week 3 and had to knock them down. Seattle has navigated some offseason losses (Klint Kubiak, Kenneth Walker III and more) and injury issues (the entire backfield), and three of its four losses came in one-score games, but we expected the Seahawks to be closer to the top of the division than they are right now.

The Bills have overcome a questionable defense to emerge midway through the season with a 7-1 record. Josh Allen is firmly in the MVP mix once again. James Cook is averaging even more rushing yards per game than he did a year ago. The offense has kept humming despite DJ Moore missing time. The Joe Brady era is off to a very good start.

The Dolphins have played right around expectations so far this year. They have smartly played at a snail's pace on offense to try and shorten games and stay competitive, which has resulted in them losing by less than expected in some contests, and they even beat the Jets. Still, it's hard to justify better than a 'C' grade when you're 1-7 at the halfway point.

The Patriots' start to the season was terrible. They then got on a little bit of a run to bounce back, and it looked like they might recapture some of what they had last year. But they've lost two games against good teams over the last three weeks, and they got smacked by the Packers in the most recent one. The injury issues on offense matter, but sitting at 5-4 before their trip to Munich is a slight disappointment.

The Jets look like they have a nice corps of young players on both offense and defense, but they're also 2-7. It's hard to find the appropriate grade for that type of team, especially when it's coming off its worst loss of the season, where it was totally non-competitive. It feels like a 'C+' is just right, relative to what we expected from them coming into this year.

Considering they haven't had Lamar Jackson for much of the season (he basically played 3.5 games), it's at least somewhat impressive that the Ravens are still in the mix in the AFC at 4-5. But they've lost four games in a row and have looked inept offensively of late (albeit in brutal situations), and Jesse Minter's defense hasn't been able to make up for it.

The Bengals' offense started the season somewhat slowly, as per usual, but has kicked into high gear of late, as per usual. Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are basically unstoppable, and the defense is improved relative to recent years. There have been some ups and downs with that unit (27 points against the Bucs despite four turnovers, 30 against the Steelers, 24 against the Dolphins despite three turnovers, 36 against the Titans despite two turnovers), so that's keeping them from earning a straight 'A' here.

The Browns are 5-4, which would make you think they should get an 'A' relative to expectations. But when you look at the context of those games, and the fact that they each required a game-winning drive in the final five minutes, you see that the record isn't as impressive as it looks on the surface. Still, the wins count, and five is probably more than many people expected them to get coming into the year.

The inexcusable loss to the Browns back in Week 4 keeps the Steelers out of the 'A' range, which they might otherwise be in, given their offense and defense. The run game has been impressive, and the defense has maintained a high level of play. Coming out of their bye at 6-2 is an ideal midseason result.

The Texans are 3-5, and two of their wins have come against the Titans and Chargers. Their defense has regressed year over year. That all overshadows the great season they're getting out of C.J. Stroud, who has been even better this year than he was during his spectacular rookie season.

The Colts have been a disaster on both sides of the ball and had to enter fire-sale mode. This grade would be lower if not for the fact that they did get some assets for a few players who were obviously on their way out the door.

The Jaguars are 6-2 with two one-score losses, and they look elite on both offense and defense. They might have an inside track on the No. 1 seed in the AFC, given their rest-of-season strength of schedule. We docked them to an 'A-' thanks only to the frankly bonkers price they paid in the Jordan Davis trade, even if he is going to help their defense the rest of the way.

The Titans looked more competent in their final three games going into their Week 9 bye, even if they did lose two of them. The offense looked so bad early in the year, though, that we can't even justify giving them a straight 'C' here. We're grading the entire season to date, not just what's happened most recently. Getting a second-round pick and more for Amani Hooker was nice, though.

I don't know how the Broncos keep getting away with it in one-score games (6-0 this season), but they do. They're probably not as good as their 6-2 record suggests, and they got embarrassed in the season opener against Kansas City, but there's no denying their track record of winning in clutch situations at this point. So, we're giving them a bit of credit for it here.

The Chiefs have taken care of business for the most part this season, losing only to the Seahawks and Broncos on the road in back-to-back weeks. They have otherwise been able to run the ball at will on everyone, and their defense has been excellent. The blip in Weeks 7 and 8 counts, though, and it revealed an inability to find a way to win if Kenneth Walker doesn't go off. That matters.

Things worked out quite nicely for the Raiders. They started out 3-0, Kirk Cousins played well enough to give Fernando Mendoza time to sit and learn for half a season, and then they got a third-round pick for Cousins at the deadline. If they hadn't lost five of their last six games, this grade would be even higher.

#2525. Germany boss confident Musiala will return to his best despite Hoeneß doubts

Germany sporting director Rudi Völler has backed Jamal Musiala to return to top form following a series of setbacks for the Bayern Munich midfielder in recent years.

Musiala missed the start of the season after suffering on-field collapses linked to a neurological condition. Upon his return, he then sustained a muscle fibre tear that has kept him sidelined for more than a month.

Nevertheless, Völler has no doubts that the 23-year-old will bounce back and rediscover his best form.

"Based on the information I have, I am convinced that he will come back as strong as he was before the injury. There is no reason to be sceptical about that. I am absolutely convinced that we will see Jamal Musiala in outstanding form at many, many tournaments – he is still very young, after all," Völler said on DAZN's “Never Talk Alone” programme.

This season's concerns follow a horrific fibula fracture Musiala suffered after colliding with Gianluigi Donnarumma during Bayern Munich's Club World Cup quarter-final against Paris Saint-Germain in the summer of 2025. The injury kept him out of action for several months.

"Unfortunately, he was also unlucky back then with Donnarumma, when he suffered a serious ankle injury and had to undergo surgery. It really was a very, very serious injury. He needs some time to get back to where he was. And if he can avoid further problems like that, I am completely optimistic that he will be able to produce top-level performances again," Völler said.

Regarding Musiala's neurological condition, Völler said he would be more concerned about recurring muscle injuries.

“It's not something you see every day in professional sport, but I actually thought it was a good thing that it became public and that it's being handled sensibly," he said.

Bayern supervisory board member Uli Hoeneß recently described Musiala's situation as a dilemma for the club, raising doubts over whether the midfielder will ever return to his previous level.

"Just imagine if Bayern Munich were now to question his contract and say: What he is capable of delivering now is no longer what is stipulated in the contract," Hoeneß told BR.

Völler, however, doesn't think too much should be read into Hoeneß's comments.

“I don't see it as that dramatic. These are just things – we all know Uli. Perhaps he also likes to provoke people a little in his own way. But he never really means any harm. That has always been one of his great strengths, even over all these decades: he goes out of his way to protect his own players and support them,” he said.

"With one player, he might be particularly complimentary; with another, he might be a little more critical. But fundamentally, he loves them all."

#2524. Caleb Wilson reportedly out 4-6 weeks with broken hand, taking away the only reason to watch the Bulls

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA injury train is showing no signs of slowing down as Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson will undergo surgery for a fractured right hand and miss four to six weeks of action, according to ESPN.

Wilson, the No. 4 pick in the 2026 NBA Draft, was injured in Wednesday night's loss to the Spurs. He was off to a great start for the otherwise struggling Bulls, who are now 1-9. He's an electric watch as a 6-foot-9, gliding athlete with every tool in the kit. He's averaging 18.9 points, 6.2 boards and nearly two steals a night so far. Before the injury, Wilson was listed at 15-1 to win Rookie of the Year, but within minutes of the news of his injury surfacing, those odds fell to 40-1 at FanDuel.

Before the injury, those were the fifth-best odds, which in most classes might not sound like a player having as good a start as Wilson, but this is an absolutely stacked rookie class with Yaxel Lendeborg being an actual All-Star candidate, Darius Acuff Jr. averaging over 26 points per game, Darryn Peterson averaging over 23 points in his last four and Cameron Boozer stuffing the stat sheet at 15.9 points, 9.8 rebounds and 5.5 assists a night for a Grizzlies team on the rise.

Wilson is the future in Chicago, and in the long term, that's all that matters. They almost have to look to trade Norman Powell before the deadline, and Nic Claxton should join him on the way out. Powell's deal is particularly priced to be moved as next year's $22.5 million is a team option. That's a good number for a player of Powell's worth but could also be an expiring deal for a team looking to use him for a championship push and then reassess over the summer with no long-term commitment.

However that plays out, the next month and change is going to be even more brutal for Bulls fans than the first three weeks of the season have been now that Wilson, like so many other of the league's most exciting players, is headed for street clothes.

This news of Wilson's injury comes on the same day that the Warriors listed Stephen Curry out for at least the next two weeks with an oblique tear. From Anthony Edwards to Jalen Williams, Tyrese Haliburton, Jaren Jackson Jr., Ja Morant, Kawhi Leonard, Cason Wallace, Paolo Banchero, Chet Holmgren, Jalen Duren, Curry and beyond, this is a massive issue that the NBA, in some capacity, needs to take meaningful steps toward at least attempting to resolve.

Fans are paying way too much money not to watch the best players, and for the Bulls, Wilson was the main attraction for a team that will struggle to win games. Outside of diehards who are going to tune in no matter what, absolutely no casual fan has an interest in watching Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis on a 1-9 team. That's the harsh truth.

#2522. Rockets' Marcus Smart suspended three games for punching Warriors' Charles Bassey during in-game scuffle

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA has suspended Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart for three games for "throwing a punch that made contact with the face" of Golden State Warriors big man Charles Bassey, the league announced on Thursday.

The incident came late in the third quarter of Wednesday night's game in Houston. After Smart and Bassey got tangled up on the other end of the floor, Smart chased Bassey down and threw a punch at his head area. They were quickly broken up from there, and Smart was eventually ejected from the game with a flagrant-2 foul. Despite his absence, the Rockets went on to win the game, 115-108.

MARCUS SMART PUNCHES CHARLES BASSEY 😳 pic.twitter.com/MUsLlDHCz4

What triggered the incident? "I just talked to [Smart]. He said they got wrapped up, and [Smart]'s elbow that he hurt got bent up," Rockets coach Ime Udoka said after the game. "So, [Smart] said something to him. Bassey said, 'What are you going to do?' And he did it."

Bassey, on the other hand, blamed Smart for what happened. "He's been playing dirty the whole game," the Warriors big man said. "In the first half, I was trying to set a screen and he grabbed my knee. So I mean, he was playing dirty. [On the play in question], I think I was trying to get a rebound and he was grabbing my hand and I was trying to run back on defense. ... And then he got up on me and swung. Obviously that was weak. I think that was, honestly, fake toughness."

Charles Bassey on Marcus Smart throwing a punch at him: “Fake toughness.”“I don’t think he was trying to play. I think he was trying to get himself out of the game.” pic.twitter.com/ZxbgvUDeY9

As for what sort of words were exchanged between Smart and Bassey? "He said something to me," Bassey explained. "He said something like, 'Hey, don't do that.' I said, 'Do what?' It's a grown-man's league."

Smart is no stranger to NBA discipline. He has 12 ejections, nine fines (excluding flopping and technical foul fines) and two suspensions across his 13-year career. Now, the 9-3 Rockets will be without a key guard for the next three games, but fortunately for them, their next three opponents are all below .500: the Utah Jazz, Washington Wizards and Miami Heat.
